orient: Narrator: Nelly Dean, continuing her story to Lockwood. The chapter opens in 1797, just after Heathcliff has taken his son Linton away to Wuthering Heights, then jumps ahead to young Cathy's sixteenth birthday, which scholars date to 20 March 1800.

notes.g: Young Catherine Linton, Edgar's daughter, whom Nelly is raising.
notes.n: Not her mother, Catherine Earnshaw. In this part of the story 'Catherine' and 'Cathy' always mean the daughter.

notes.g: Edgar Linton, Cathy's father and Nelly's master at Thrushcross Grange.

notes.n: Heathcliff took the boy to Wuthering Heights the morning after he arrived at the Grange (Chapter XX), so Edgar has little hope.

notes.g: Time worked better at healing her grief.
Linton Heathcliff, Cathy's sickly cousin: son of Heathcliff and Edgar's late sister Isabella.
notes.n: Careful: 'Mr. Linton' in this chapter means Edgar, Cathy's father.
'Wax' means grow, as in the waxing moon.
Nelly says below that this woman later left and was replaced.

notes.g: The nearby village, with the church, shops and doctor.
The master of Wuthering Heights, Linton's father.
Young Cathy, who hardly ever left the Grange park.
A tiresome person to live with.
notes.m: 'Inmate' just meant someone living in a house, not a prisoner or patient.

notes.t: could not do at all with
notes.g: Couldn't put up with at all.
For many minutes at a stretch.

notes.m: 'Apartment' meant a single room, not a flat.

notes.n: Separate from 'the house', the big main room where the family, servants and visitors gather.

notes.t: it’s killing, a breath of night air
notes.n: Many people then believed night air was unhealthy and carried disease.

notes.g: The sour old servant at Wuthering Heights, always quoting the Bible.
Short of food and comforts in winter.
A drink for invalids: toasted bread soaked in hot water.
notes.n: It was thought to be soothing and easy on a weak stomach.

notes.g: A shelf beside the fire for keeping pots and drinks warm.
Hareton Earnshaw, Hindley's son: Cathy's other cousin, raised rough and unschooled by Heathcliff.
notes.n: Cathy met him on her trip to Penistone Crags (Chapter XVIII).

notes.t: Earnshaw’s thrashing him to a mummy
notes.g: Hareton beating him to a pulp.
notes.n: 'Earnshaw' here means Hareton. 'Beat to a mummy' was an old phrase for beating someone into a soft, crushed mess.

notes.t: fit to turn him out of doors
notes.g: Ready to throw him out of the house.
Put himself where he'd be tempted (to hurt Linton).
notes.n: An echo of the Lord's Prayer: 'lead us not into temptation'.

notes.t: in the house where he is
notes.g: In the main living room ('the house') when Heathcliff is in it.

notes.m: Means immediately, not 'in a straight line'.

notes.g: His fate; his situation in life.

notes.m: British for exhausted. Not the American slang for pregnant.

notes.t: was her successor; she lives there still
notes.g: The new housekeeper, still working there in 1801.
notes.n: Presumably Zillah, the stout housekeeper Lockwood met in Chapter II.
Scholars date this birthday to 20 March 1800.

notes.g: The death of Cathy's mother, Catherine.
notes.n: 'Late' means dead. Catherine died a few hours after giving birth to Cathy (Chapter XVI).

notes.g: Gimmerton churchyard, where Catherine is buried.
notes.n: 'Kirk' is the northern and Scottish word for church.

notes.g: Had withdrawn to a private room.
Nelly Dean, the narrator. Cathy uses her proper first name.
Red grouse, wild birds of the heather moors.
notes.n: Prized game birds, shot for sport in autumn. They nest on the ground among the heather.

notes.g: A woman's hat, tied under the chin.

notes.n: A 'sally' was first a soldiers' rush out of a besieged fort.

notes.g: Skylarks: small brown birds that sing as they fly high up.

notes.t: It’s a pity she could not be content.
notes.n: She tells this story knowing what came after. Keep the remark in mind.

notes.g: The fence around the Grange's park.
notes.n: A 'park' is the large enclosed grounds of a country house.

notes.g: Flushed the birds out of hiding.

notes.n: The two houses are roughly four miles apart.

notes.m: Just to halt someone, not a police arrest.

notes.g: The moor-game: plump wild birds shot for sport.
Heathcliff owns the moor around his house, and the game on it.
notes.n: Wild game belonged to the landowner. Taking birds or eggs was poaching, a crime that could be harshly punished.

notes.g: Scolding the trespasser who was after his game.
To back up what she said.
That he knew who we were.
The Lintons' house, where Cathy and Nelly live.

notes.n: Heathcliff is sneering.

notes.g: Cathy met Hareton on her trip to Penistone Crags (Chapter XVIII).

notes.t: gained nothing but increased bulk and strength

notes.m: 'Presently' meant 'before long', not 'at present'.
A 'nurse' looked after children; not a medical nurse.

notes.n: 'Nab' is a northern word for a jutting hilltop or rocky point.

notes.g: The rocky outcrop on the moors that Cathy longed to visit (Chapter XVIII).
Wuthering Heights, where Nelly found her in Chapter XVIII.
Go on ahead with the girl.
The stone slabs at the house door.
The top edge of the slope.
Hareton, who had been told to go with her.

notes.m: 'Pretend' here means attempt or claim, not fake.

notes.g: Veered away, like a startled horse.

notes.m: 'Suffer' meant 'permit', not 'feel pain'.

notes.t: That the two cousins may fall in love, and get married.
notes.n: Marriage between first cousins was legal and fairly common then, especially among families with property.
'Chit' is a dismissive word for a young girl.

notes.g: Has no inheritance to look forward to.
notes.m: 'Expectations' meant what you expected to inherit, as in Dickens's 'Great Expectations'.
notes.n: In Chapter X, Nelly explained that without a son, Edgar's property might pass to Isabella's side of the family.

notes.g: Sharing the inheritance with Linton, as his wife.
Nelly means Cathy would inherit Linton's share.

notes.t: no clause in the will to secure it so
notes.g: Nothing in the will guarantees that.
notes.n: Heathcliff says that if Linton died, his property would pass to his father, not to Cathy. A marriage would avoid any quarrel over it.

notes.m: 'Returned' here means answered, not came back.

notes.n: Nelly hopes his old feeling for the mother will make him gentle with the daughter.

notes.t: disarm him from desiring her injury
notes.g: Stop him from wanting to harm her.

notes.t: still wanting some months of sixteen
notes.g: Still a few months short of sixteen.

notes.m: 'Genial' here describes kindly, warm weather, not a friendly person.

notes.t: that you used to tease us so with wishing to see
notes.g: Whom you kept pestering us about, wanting to see her.

notes.m: 'Without' here means outside, the opposite of 'within'.
notes.n: Heathcliff pretends to look out of the door but is really watching the cousins.

notes.m: To 'salute' meant to greet with a kiss, not a military salute.

notes.g: Heathcliff is her uncle by marriage: he married her father's sister Isabella.

notes.t: once or twice too often before you were born
notes.g: Heathcliff means his visits to her mother at the Grange.
notes.n: Those visits ended in the violent quarrels of Chapters X to XV.

notes.g: A pained face he could barely hide.

notes.t: careless of seeing your cousin hereafter
notes.g: Don't care whether you see your cousin again.

notes.t: He thought me too poor to wed his sister
notes.n: Edgar did object to Heathcliff's low, unknown birth, but above all to his character (Chapter X). Isabella ran off with him (Chapter XII).

notes.g: Find out how little he's worth.
Long to have as my own.
However low he has been brought.
In no danger of her falling for him.

notes.t: pit him against that paltry creature
notes.g: Set Hareton up as a rival to that feeble boy.

notes.n: Heathcliff calls his own son 'it', as if he were a thing.

notes.t: We calculate it will scarcely last till it is eighteen
notes.g: We reckon he'll hardly live to eighteen.
notes.n: Heathcliff's cold guess about his own son's health.

notes.g: What the Heights housekeeper had told her.
notes.n: In Chapter XVIII she told Cathy that Hareton was her cousin, which upset Cathy badly.

notes.g: Hareton's father, Hindley, was the brother of Cathy's mother.

notes.m: 'Queer' meant odd or peculiar.

notes.t: a dim notion of his inferiority
notes.g: A vague sense that he was looked down on.
Heathcliff is both Hareton's employer and the man who took charge of him.
notes.n: He took the boy when Hindley died (Chapter XVII).
In Chapter XVII Nelly said Hareton should have been 'the first gentleman in the neighbourhood'. Instead he has been raised as a farmhand.

notes.g: Made him too shy to speak.

notes.n: The same word as modern British 'gormless'.

notes.m: Today 'bathos' means a silly anticlimax. Heathcliff uses the Greek root sense, 'depth'.

notes.t: faster than his scoundrel of a father secured me
notes.g: More firmly than his villain of a father, Hindley, held me down.
notes.n: Hindley degraded the young Heathcliff after old Mr. Earnshaw died (Chapter VI). Now Heathcliff does the same to Hindley's son.

notes.g: Beyond the animal: anything of the mind or spirit.
Hindley Earnshaw, Hareton's father and Heathcliff's old enemy, now dead (Chapter XVII).

notes.t: gold put to the use of paving-stones
notes.g: Hareton: something precious wasted on a lowly use.

notes.t: tin polished to ape a service of silver
notes.g: Linton: cheap stuff polished up to imitate a silver dinner set.
notes.n: 'Ape' means imitate; a 'service' is a full set of tableware.

notes.t: he would have more than any, but I, are aware of
notes.g: Hindley would have more to regret than anyone except me knows.

notes.m: 'Own' here means admit or confess.
'Remark' meant notice, not comment aloud.

notes.g: A row of beehives on a stand.
notes.n: Farms kept bees for honey and wax.

notes.g: The window, made of small panes set in a criss-cross frame.
The carving Lockwood saw in Chapter I: the date '1500' and the name 'Hareton Earnshaw'.
notes.n: So Hareton cannot read his own name, carved over the door of his family's old house.

notes.m: A 'clown' was a clumsy rustic or peasant, not a circus performer.

notes.g: Can't read; doesn't know the alphabet.

notes.m: 'Simple' meant feeble-minded, not plain or easy.

notes.n: Linton is mocking Hareton's accent.
He grew up in the south with his mother, near London (Chapter XVII).
Hareton means: what's the use of reading?

notes.s: If thou weren’t more a lass
notes.tr: If you weren't more of a girl than a boy, I'd knock you down this minute, I would, you pathetic stick of a creature!

notes.g: A thin strip of wood; here, a skinny weakling.

notes.m: 'Partial' here means unfair, not 'incomplete' or 'fond of'.
'Start' here means flinch, not begin.
'Faithful' here means true to the facts.

notes.g: Edgar's sister and Linton's mother, who died in the south (Chapter XIX).

notes.t: a hasty sketch of his conduct to Isabella
notes.g: A quick account of how Heathcliff treated his wife.
notes.n: Told in Chapters XII to XVII.

notes.t: the manner in which Wuthering Heights became his property
notes.n: Hindley mortgaged the house to Heathcliff to pay his gambling debts, so it passed to him when Hindley died (Chapter XVII).

notes.m: 'Ancient' here just means from long ago, not thousands of years old.

notes.g: The death of Edgar's wife Catherine, Cathy's mother.

notes.t: She might have been living yet, if it had not been for him!
notes.g: Edgar blames Heathcliff for Catherine's final illness.
notes.n: See Chapters XI to XVI.

notes.m: 'Prosecute' meant to pursue or carry on, not to take to court.

notes.g: Small setback; something going against you.
Look! An old exclamation of surprise.

notes.n: Servants often called a daughter of the house simply 'Miss'.

notes.g: A small metal cone for putting out a candle; a snuffer.
Locked her door from the inside by sliding the bolt.

notes.n: 'Humour' meant mood.

notes.g: A boy who came from the village to collect milk from the Grange.
notes.n: The Grange has its own dairy, and villagers bought milk there.

notes.g: Beyond the pages of the book.

notes.t: borrowed from a more experienced source
notes.g: Nelly suspects someone older helped write them.
notes.n: She does not say whom she suspects.

notes.m: 'Affected' here means artificial or showy, not 'influenced'.

notes.g: A servant who milks cows and makes butter and cheese.

notes.m: To 'abstract' meant to remove or steal, not to summarise.
Today 'peruse' is often used to mean skim. Here it means read thoroughly.
'Work' here means needlework.

notes.g: A nest whose eggs or chicks have been stolen.
notes.n: Nelly's simile recalls the grouse nests Cathy went hunting at the start of the chapter.

notes.g: Her face, happy until a moment ago.
notes.m: 'Late' here means recent, not dead or tardy.
In Britain 'corn' meant wheat, oats or barley, not American corn (maize).

notes.g: A fine sort of love, I must say!
notes.n: Said sarcastically.

notes.g: Thought it was all silly girlish nonsense.
notes.n: 'Vanity' here means something empty and foolish.

notes.g: Lovers often exchanged locks of hair as keepsakes.

notes.m: 'Dinner' was the main meal, eaten around the middle of the day.

notes.g: Came back at teatime, the light late-afternoon meal.

notes.n: 'Master' was the polite title for a boy, as 'Mister' was for a man.

notes.g: Cathy's formal name, as Edgar Linton's daughter.
